Topics in Biology: Dynamics of Society in Nature. This seminar dives into the dynamic and often counter-intuitive relationship between society and nature. This is sometimes referred to as coupled human-natural systems or CHANS, and also as social-ecological systems. This is the underlying theory and science of sustainability. The course material will help you to think about the convergence of natural science, ecological economics, and sociocultural value systems, an essential step in connecting science to policy directives and sustainable behavior at governance levels from villages to international superpowers. We will examine this convergence through an existing policy rubric, the SDG (sustainable development goal), and a series of in-depth case studies drawing from both the Global North (US and Australia- renewable energy and ecosystem-based management in the coastal ocean) as compared to parallel problems being dealt with in the Global South (here, the Caribbean, East Africa, and the Mekong Basin in Cambodia). The flows of services and production of materials that connect nature and society are called “ecosystem services”. The course is conducted in a mixed lecture/seminar format, calling upon the students to actively participate in workshopping environmental solutions based on background readings. It will be especially useful and fun for students with an interest in practical aspects of STEM disciplines, the social sciences, and both together. Interests in related arts are also encouraged as a means of expression, but are not the focus of this course.

Topics in Biology: Dynamics of Society in Nature. This seminar dives into the dynamic and often counter-intuitive relationship between society and nature. This is sometimes referred to as coupled human-natural systems or CHANS, and also as social-ecological systems. This is the underlying theory and science of sustainability. The course material will help you to think about the convergence of natural science, ecological economics, and sociocultural value systems, an essential step in connecting science to policy directives and sustainable behavior at governance levels from villages to international superpowers. We will examine this convergence through an existing policy rubric, the SDG (sustainable development goal), and a series of in-depth case studies drawing from both the Global North (US and Australia- renewable energy and ecosystem-based management in the coastal ocean) as compared to parallel problems being dealt with in the Global South (here, the Caribbean, East Africa, and the Mekong Basin in Cambodia). The flows of services and production of materials that connect nature and society are called “ecosystem services”. The course is conducted in a mixed lecture/seminar format, calling upon the students to actively participate in workshopping environmental solutions based on background readings. It will be especially useful and fun for students with an interest in practical aspects of STEM disciplines, the social sciences, and both together. Interests in related arts are also encouraged as a means of expression, but are not the focus of this course.
